stemMd: In the second paragraph, buyers "will discount every bottle accordingly." As used here, "discount" most nearly means that buyers

options.label: A
options.textMd: refuse to buy any bottle whose quality they cannot check first.

options.label: B
options.textMd: sell bottles on to other shoppers at a lower price than they paid.

options.label: C
options.textMd: ignore the price and choose each bottle by the taste of the oil.

options.label: D
options.textMd: lower the price they offer, allowing for the risk of poor oil.

options.label: E
options.textMd: ask each seller for a reduction on the price shown in the shop.

explanationMd:
For meaning-in-context questions, set aside the sense you know best (a shop's discount) and reread the sentence around the word. The whole sentence is: if buyers cannot tell good oil from mediocre oil, "they will offer a price that reflects the average quality they expect, and they will discount every bottle accordingly". The buyers are the ones acting, and what they do is lower the price they offer because they doubt the quality. To "discount" a bottle is therefore to value it at less than its best case, allowing for the chance of disappointment.

Check by substituting each choice into the sentence and reading on. The next sentences say the price offered falls and careful producers are paid less than their oil is worth, so buyers are still buying, at a lower valuation. Refusing to buy would leave no price to fall; haggling with each seller brings in a bargaining scene the passage never describes; reselling at a loss turns the buyers into sellers; and choosing by taste is impossible, since the passage says quality can be judged only after paying.

distractorRationale.e: This gives "discount" its everyday shop meaning, a reduction the seller grants at the till. In the passage no one bargains: the buyers themselves lower what they are prepared to offer.
distractorRationale.a: Buyers in the passage still buy, at a lower price, even though they cannot check quality first. Refusing to buy would leave no market in which the offered price could keep falling, as the paragraph says it does.
distractorRationale.c: Buyers cannot taste the oil before paying, which is the whole problem the passage describes, so they cannot choose bottles by taste; and the paragraph is about the price they offer, so the price is not ignored.
distractorRationale.b: This reads the buyers as traders passing bottles on at a loss. Nothing in the passage concerns resale; the buyers are shoppers deciding what to offer.

accessibilityText: A meaning-in-context question about the olive oil passage. It asks what "discount" most nearly means in the second-paragraph phrase "they will discount every bottle accordingly". The five choices say that buyers: refuse to buy any bottle whose quality they cannot check first; sell bottles on to other shoppers at a lower price than they paid; ignore the price and choose each bottle by the taste of the oil; lower the price they offer, allowing for the risk of poor oil; ask each seller for a reduction on the price shown in the shop.

independentSolve.workingNotes: The sentence says buyers who cannot tell quality offer a price reflecting expected average quality and discount every bottle accordingly, i.e. reduce what they are willing to pay to allow for the risk of poor oil. Refusing to buy contradicts their offering a price; reselling and ignoring price are unsupported; asking sellers for a reduction is a literal haggling sense the passage does not describe, since the discount is built into the offer rather than negotiated per bottle. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-cue-batch2-run1) reached the same answer: In context, buyers offer a price that reflects the average quality they expect, and a careful producer is then paid less than the oil is worth. So 'discount' means lowering the price offered to allow for the risk of poor oil. Refusing to buy contradicts the passage, which says buyers still buy at a lower price. Reselling, ignoring the price, and haggling in the shop for a reduction are not what the sentence describes. The haggling choice plays on the everyday sense of 'discount'.]
